Meta’s Generative Ads Model (GEM): Scaling the Central Model and Compute Engine for Frontier Ads AI
abstract: Last year, we introduced GEM , the industry’s largest recommendation system (RecSys) foundation model. GEM established Meta’s first LLM-inspired paradigm for ads recommendation, driving major performance gains. Building on this foundation, our next goal is to further scale both compute and intelligence transfer with next-generation hardware, and expand this capability across Meta’s entire ads ecosystem. This spans dozens of surfaces and objectives, delivering seamless full-funnel optimization across awareness, consideration, and conversions. The 2026 generation of GEM shifts from isolated per-domain optimizations — such as Facebook, Instagram, Reels — to a single central foundation model. It learns from data and signals across all of Meta’s ads platforms, bends the scaling curve at LLM-scale computation, and delivers strong advertiser outcomes through post-training techniques that provide a larger latency budget without requiring real-time evaluation of all ad candidates — all on a substantially more efficient training stack. The result is simultaneous ad performance gains across every surface and funnel stage, and deeper understanding that better matches ads to what people are looking for. GEM has delivered 18.9% conversion improvement and 12% ad click-through rate (CTR) improvement across Meta’s ad surfaces and objectives, and additionally contributed 5.8%, 4.1%, and 1.6% conversion uplift on Facebook, Instagram, and off-site conversion for targeted users over the past year. These gains span both upper-funnel surfaces and deep-funnel optimization goals, driving stronger returns for advertisers. GEM advances the frontier of recommender systems in the following four areas: 1. Bending the Scaling Curve, Enabling 2.5x Model Complexity Challenge: Empirical scaling laws demonstrate that model performance predictably improves with compute, parameter, and data size using transformer model architecture. However, recommender system models do not exhibit similar scaling properties with transformer due to massive heterogeneous features and shifting distributions. Solution: We built an LLM-style architecture — Kunlun , co-designed with the latest GPU hardware, to make larger, deeper models substantially more cost-efficient and to enable long-context learning over user engagement history. We observed an LLM-like scaling law at our largest pre-training scale with 2.5x model complexity growth from earlier versions of GEM. The pattern mirrors frontier LLMs: more capacity and longer context produce emergent gains in ranking quality that translate directly into business results. 2. Efficient Intelligence Transfer From GEM to User-Facing Models Challenge: Serving a model at this scale in real time is prohibitively expensive and drives up latency, compromising both user experience and advertiser ROI. Solution: The structured representation, LoopFM , a state-of-the-art post-training technique, transfers GEM’s internal representations and sequential historical memory to downstream models. Through computation sharing, it doubles the intelligence transfer together with the knowledge distillation deployed in the previous version, at no additional compute cost or latency. We also introduced elastic pre-computation ( Solaris ) to harvest the gains from the upstream model. 3. Accelerating the Central Compute Engine With Large-Scale Cross-Surface, Cross-Domain Learning at Meta Ads Scale Challenge: Meta’s apps span dozens of surfaces — Facebook, Instagram, Reels, Stories, and more — with 3.6 billion people using at least one of our apps each day. Each surface and optimization objective previously had its own independent prediction system. As the platform grows in surfaces and objectives, so does the challenge of improving ad performance simultaneously. title: Building agents that transact with Anchor Browser and AgentCore payments
abstract: AI agents increasingly need to access web resources that are priced per request. For example, premium datasets charge by the query, research APIs meter by the call, and paywalled publishers gate content behind payment. When an AI agent encounters one of these resources, the server returns HTTP 402 Payment Required. The agent has no built-in payment mechanism, no budget attached to the session, and no programmatic way to satisfy the request. The task stalls and requires manual intervention. Anchor Browser with Agentic Payments handles machine-to-machine payment workflows on behalf of the agent. Developed in collaboration with the AWS Generative AI Innovation Center Partner Agent Factory , it’s now available on AWS Marketplace . This post covers how Anchor Browser integrates with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore payments so that AI agents can pay for x402-protected pages and APIs autonomously. The x402 protocol is an open standard for HTTP-based machine-to-machine payments. A server responds with 402 Payment Required along with the amount, accepted payment methods, and payment address that the agent uses to complete the transaction. Anchor Browser is a cloud-based browser automation solution purpose-built for AI agents. Each agent session runs inside a managed browser environment that maintains authentication state, handles navigation, captures network requests, and provides a live view of page interactions. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore provides capabilities to build, connect, and optimize agents at scale. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore payments is a fully managed capability within AgentCore that AI agents can use to discover, access, and pay for APIs, Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers, and web content autonomously. AgentCore payments manages wallet connectivity, enforces configurable spending limits at the infrastructure layer, and processes payments through the x402 protocol. It also provides observability into payment attempts, approvals, denials, and settlements through Amazon CloudWatch. When an agent running in Anchor Browser encounters a 402 response, AgentCore payments authorizes and completes the transaction within the configured budget. The workflow continues without interruption. Challenges When an autonomous agent encounters an x402-protected resource, the workflow stalls. The agent makes a request, such as fetching a premium research report or calling a paid data enrichment API, and the server responds with HTTP 402 Payment Required. Without a mechanism to pay, the task that was supposed to run autonomously now requires human intervention. Today, developers must build the entire payment stack. This effort spans four categories of complexity: Payment protocol handling Detecting and parsing the 402 challenge from the HTTP response, and distinguishing payment-required responses from other 4xx errors. Constructing the correct payment header with the cryptographic proof in the exact format the merchant expects. Supporting multiple payment schemes (exact, upto, and protocol variants) without hardcoding vendor-specific logic into the agent. Maintaining compatibility across x402 merchant implementations that might vary in challenge format, supported stablecoins, or settlement timing. Security and key management Storing a private key to sign payments, requiring secure key storage within an environment exposed to untrusted inputs. Managing wallet lifecycle operations, including key rotation, credential refresh, and provider failover. Operational resilience Resubmitting the original request with the payment header while preserving session state, cookies, and request context. Providing idempotency, which is essential for wallet operations. Enforcing per-session and per-transaction spend limits with real-time budget tracking across concurrent agent executions. title: Manage private pricing offers for Amazon Bedrock with managed entitlements
abstract: Managing AI model access across dozens or hundreds of AWS accounts creates operational friction when each workload account must subscribe and accept AWS Marketplace Private Pricing Offers (MPPOs) individually. Amazon Bedrock with managed entitlements simplifies multi-account access to third-party AI models so you can subscribe once from a central account and distribute access across your organization. In this post, we show you two ways to activate AWS Marketplace Private Pricing Offer (MPPO) entitlements in AWS License Manager. Use the lightweight script when you want a one-time, no-infrastructure fix for received licenses you already trust. Use the CDK automation when you want ongoing event-driven processing that verifies sellers, creates and activates distributed grants. Why automate grant activation With AWS Marketplace Private Pricing Offers, you can negotiate custom rates for third-party models on Amazon Bedrock. After an eligible private offer is accepted, AWS Marketplace creates a license in AWS License Manager. In AWS Organizations with all features enabled, organization-level grants are auto-accepted but remain Disabled until you activate them. Teams often manage this by checking the AWS License Manager console and activating grants manually. Manual checks work, but they add effort and are easy to miss. Until someone activates the grant, negotiated pricing does not apply. The same effort appears as teams adopt new models or renew terms. Solution overview The sample repository provides two paths: Path 1 – The lightweight path is a standalone script that lists received licenses and prints a dry-run plan. It only creates and activates organization-wide grants when you re-run it with --apply --confirm-account-id . It has no seller allow-list, so use it only when you trust every received license in the management account. Path 2 – The event-driven path uses AWS Cloud Development Kit (AWS CDK) to deploy ongoing automation in your AWS management account. Choose one of the following implementation paths. Use Path 1 for one-time activation without CDK. Use Path 2 for ongoing event-driven automation. Path 1: Lightweight script (one-time activation) Use this path when you need one-time activation without deploying CDK. The script lists every received license in the management account, so use the dry run as your review gate before applying changes. Clone the sample repository locally and move into the project directory. git clone https://github.com/aws-samples/sample-bedrock-managed-entitlements.git cd sample-bedrock-managed-entitlements Run the lightweight script in dry-run mode. python3 lightweight/distribute_licenses.py Review every listed license and confirm that the ISV Partner issuer and account scope match the private offer you expect. Billing data in AWS Cost Explorer can lag, so use it to compare the effective charge for covered Amazon Bedrock usage after charges appear. For a repeatable check, adapt the sample scripts/bedrock_discount_check.py utility to match your ISV Partner issuer and confirm the expected discount path. Path 2: CDK automation (ongoing activation) Use this path when you want new private pricing agreements handled automatically. title: Natural language security queries at Orca Security using Amazon Bedrock
abstract: Security analysts need fast answers about their cloud infrastructure without deep familiarity with domain-specific query languages. Orca Security ’s tool covers over 900 cloud models (the resource types Sonar tracks, such as an Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) instance or an Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) bucket). Querying that data required precise model names, nested relationship navigation, and selection from 18 operators (comparison functions like equals or contains used to filter results). To solve this, Orca Security partnered with AWS to build Discovery AI, a natural language query agent on Amazon Bedrock . Orca provides context-aware security for cloud, code, and AI, and Sonar is its domain-specific query system where users search, filter, and explore across the entire data graph. In this post, we share the architecture and results of Discovery AI, which converts a natural language question into a Sonar query. As a result, Orca reduced query costs by 90 percent, input tokens by 93 percent, and latency by 75 percent compared to the initial baseline. Bridging natural language and structured queries Orca Security’s Sonar query system supports 900+ cloud infrastructure and application models with complex relationships between them. To query this data, users construct JSON objects that specify exact model names, select from 18 operators, and navigate parent-child hierarchies across cloud providers. Doing this well requires deep familiarity with the Sonar schema. To build this capability, the Orca team set out to build a natural language interface that can generate valid Sonar queries from plain text. Their initial proof of concept loaded the full Sonar schema into a single prompt on the largest available model. This included over 900 model definitions, every relationship type, and a generous set of example queries. The output quality was strong (design partners and internal users responded positively) but three significant drawbacks emerged at production scale. Token consumption was inefficient, at roughly 2 million input tokens per workload, which drove up cost. Latency was high, with end-to-end response times of around 60 seconds per workload. Accuracy on complex, multi-model queries was limited because nested relationships and multi-condition queries often required additional refinement. The Orca team validated that the concept worked. The next challenge was making it cost-effective, fast, and accurate enough for production. To address this, the Orca team designed and deployed a solution that handles thousands of queries per day at 15-second response times using Amazon Bedrock. Solution overview Orca designed Discovery AI as a hybrid solution on Amazon Bedrock that combines Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) with schema-aware query construction. The system converts natural language questions into valid Discovery filters through a multi-stage pipeline, with each stage matched to the most appropriate Amazon Bedrock model. Orca chose Amazon Bedrock because it provides multi-model access through a single API, letting the team allocate different foundation models to each pipeline stage without managing separate integrations. Amazon Bedrock also inherits AWS governance controls through AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM), virtual private cloud (VPC) endpoints, and AWS CloudTrail, meeting Orca’s security requirements. The model-agnostic architecture meant the team could swap in newer model versions as they became available without rearchitecting the pipeline. title: How ShipStation Global built an AI IT help desk on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
abstract: This post is co-written with Kenneth Salmon, Edward Boswell, Jack Armstrong, Robert Bahn, and Nick Ciubotariu from ShipStation Global. Answering the same IT questions and clearing routine tickets drains time that IT teams could spend elsewhere. To reclaim it, the ShipStation Global Engineering team built Deckhand , an AI-powered IT help desk agent for Slack, on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore . ShipStation Global is the leading intelligent shipping and logistics platform for small and mid-sized shippers, and it operates on a simple belief: the more efficient its teams are, the better it delivers for customers. Deckhand puts that belief to work. It answers routine IT and company questions from a curated knowledge base, reads error-message screenshots, and creates and updates Jira Service Management tickets. In this post, we discuss how ShipStation architected Deckhand, which resulted in resolving 97.5 percent of incoming channel queries while earning a 96 percent positive feedback rating by employees (Figure 1). Figure 1: 3-month channel coverage and positive feedback Business challenge The problem Deckhand solves is the one every IT team will recognize: the same questions are routinely asked, error messages are posted after business hours, and information needs to be gathered from different teams. At ShipStation Global, those conversations lived in a busy help desk Slack channel, where employees asked, and IT answered, one thread at a time. The answers usually already existed in a Confluence how-to article, on a company intranet page, or in a thread from eight months earlier. Finding them was the hard part. The channel data made the scale concrete. In the 12 months before launch: Employees posted more than 1,500 threads, and volume kept growing. With employees in the US, UK, Spain, Poland, Australia, and the Philippines, more than a fifth of questions arrived outside US business hours. Answers were split across different places: Confluence articles, intranet pages and PDFs, IT-maintained guides, and the channel’s own history. Repetitive questions consumed time that structured self-service steps could have handled. “We created Deckhand because getting help should be as simple as asking a question in Slack, not deciphering a ticket form or sending an email into the void. We believe that tickets are an indication of operational friction not productivity. Deckhand resolves common questions on the spot and, when it can’t, converts the conversation into a fully contextualized ticket with one click, improving the employee experience and freeing our team from endlessly repeating the phrase: ‘Please file a ticket.’” — Chris Collins, Senior Director IT at ShipStation Global Solution overview Deckhand works in Slack like any teammate—joining channels, reading the conversation, and drawing context from Slack profiles to answer IT questions in place. title: Build long-horizon agents with Grok 4.7 on Amazon Bedrock
abstract: SpaceXAI’s Grok 4.7 is now available on Amazon Bedrock, which offers a choice of foundation models (FMs) from multiple providers. According to SpaceXAI, Grok 4.7 is trained to work longer on more difficult tasks and knows when to check its own work. That matters most for agents, which carry a task through many steps and must verify what they find along the way. An agent that works this way has to do more than look things up. It has to form a candidate answer, check it against what it has learned, and refine it until it fits. Grok 4.7 exposes a reasoning effort setting that controls how much deliberation happens before each response, and for agent workloads a practical question is which level to run. In this post, we build a tool-calling agent on Grok 4.7 and evaluate it on three tasks that require search rather than lookup. The tasks are diagnosing a two-service outage from its alerts, scheduling maintenance under interacting constraints, and choosing an optimal set of migrations under a budget. Each task has exactly one correct answer, verified by brute force. We ran all three at every reasoning effort level, six times each, for 72 agent runs. The agent answered 67 of the 72 runs correctly. At xhigh it answered all 18 correctly, and at low it answered 15 of 18 while using about an eighth of the output tokens. That gives a clear trade-off you can tune per request, and we show how to measure it on your own tasks and how to monitor it in production. We report token counts rather than currency throughout. Token prices change, and the counts are what your own costs are derived from, so a measurement expressed in tokens stays valid. What SpaceXAI reports about Grok 4.7 According to SpaceXAI, Grok 4.7 uses a larger base model than Grok 4.6 and was trained with a longer reinforcement learning run on a harder mix of tasks. This mix is weighted toward problems that take many hours to complete. SpaceXAI reports that the model is better at verifying its own work and at managing longer context. SpaceXAI’s published benchmark results follow that emphasis. The largest reported gains over Grok 4.6 appear in the categories that measure sustained work rather than single-turn answers. title: Mixture-of-Experts kernel engineering on Amazon SageMaker AI
abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) is a sparsely-activated architecture that scales large language model (LLM) capacity while keeping per-token compute low. Because its operations account for a large share of total compute time, inefficiencies there directly raise request latency and cost. Therefore, optimizing MoE operations through kernel engineering offers the largest opportunity for performance gains. Fused MoE is a key optimization technique for the MoE architecture. A fused MoE system merges token routing, data shuffling, and specialized network calculations into a single batched operation on the GPU. This replaces executing those routing and expert computations as separate, sequential loop operations. While this provides latency advantages, it also brings complexity in kernel implementations and debugging capability. High GPU utilization for this architecture requires hardware-specific optimizations. In this post, we describe the different kernel optimizations we implemented for fused MoE models and show you how you can benefit from this work. We used a representative MoE model as our primary example. Swap-AB for WGMMA utilization To maximize tensor processing throughput, the NVIDIA Hopper architecture relies on the Warp Group Matrix Multiply Accumulate (WGMMA) instruction protocol, which executes collectively across a cooperative warpgroup of 128 threads. This operand asymmetry is fundamentally an instruction set architecture (ISA)-level property. In the underlying wgmma.mma_async assembly definition, the hardware fixes the matrix row dimension (M) at a constant scale of 64 to define its parallel thread-mapping topology. The column dimension (N) remains highly variable. Operand A strictly maps across this fixed M dimension (using registers or shared memory), and Operand B maps across the variable N dimension (through a shared memory descriptor). These operand slots are therefore structurally non-interchangeable. Consequently, peak hardware tile utilization is governed by these rigid shape encodings, requiring that the M dimension equals or exceeds 64 to prevent compute execution lanes from sitting idle. This structural preference stems from how Hopper Tensor Cores partition memory blocks. The hardware enforces a fixed minimum layout shape for the leading dimension of the first operand, locking the block height to exactly 64 (M=64). When a mathematical matrix possesses a large, continuous leading dimension in this primary slot, Hopper’s internal hardware schedulers can cleanly map and distribute data across the physical computing grid. This structural asymmetry becomes a severe performance bottleneck during the decode phase of MoE networks. In a standard MoE layer, the linear algebra governing expert computation is formulated using traditional matrix notation: A[M,K] x B[K,N] —> C[M,N] Where (M) represents the token row count (or batch size), (K) represents the hidden feature dimension, and (N) represents the expansive expert output dimension. During the decode phase, the system processes only one token per user sequence at a time. Consequently, the batch space or token row size is profoundly thin, regularly dropping to a profile where (M < 64), and frequently down to a single row (M = 1). Under this standard structural layout: Matrix (A) transforms into a thin, fragmented horizontal vector (for example, 1 x 4096). Matrix (B) (the core expert weights) remains in a large, dense vertical block (for example, 4096 x 8192). Because the row count (M) is tiny, Matrix (A) is physically incapable of filling the hardware’s fixed (64)-row layout bucket for Operand A. When the WGMMA instruction executes over this layout, it leaves a vast portion of the physical Tensor Core capacity completely starved. The silicon spends clock cycles processing empty spatial slots, leading to poor hardware utilization. In a standard dense LLM layer, weight matrices are static, unified, and perfectly contiguous. title: CASTLE: training natural language search before the first real query
abstract: How we addressed the cold-start problem for Airbnb’s natural language search by jointly generating synthetic training data — queries and relevance labels — from de-identified booking and search signals. By : Wendy Ran Wei , Hao Li , Weiwei Guo , Xiaowei Liu , Xueyin Chen , Chun How Tan , Malay Haldar , Soumyadip Banerjee , Kedar Bellare , Huiji Gao , Sanjeev Katariya , and Stephanie Moyerman Introduction Natural language search lets guests express intent in their own words, such as “romantic cabin near skiing” or “pet-friendly beach house that sleeps eight,” rather than navigating filters and categories. We needed to introduce this kind of search for Airbnb, and to have it work well from the start. However, this required training the model before we had actual user queries to train the model on, and a reasonable set of relevance labels (inferred from the queries) to map queries to matching listings. Without prior traffic, both must be synthesized from scratch. This is the cold-start problem for natural-language search. Other organizations have faced similar challenges and have created methods to address them. However, prior approaches address the need for a body of queries and the need for relevance labels separately. Passage-based methods such as InPars [1] prompt a large language model (LLM) to generate queries conditioned on a single document, then rely on additional LLM judgments to assign relevance labels, introducing a second source of error. Promptagator [2] improves query diversity using few-shot examples, but is still limited by the gap between its generation distribution and real user behavior. In this post, we describe Contrastive And Seed-guided Training for natural Language sEarch (CASTLE), our framework for jointly generating queries and producing relevance labels from Airbnb’s own de-identified booking data. Our paper describing CASTLE was accepted as a full research paper at the 35th ACM International Conference on Information and Knowledge Management, more widely known as CIKM 2026 [3]. Challenges Generating useful synthetic training data for search requires more than producing grammatically plausible queries. The distribution of synthetic queries must match how real guests actually search; their preferred phrasing, query length, and attributes they tend to mention. If queries fail to match real-world search patterns, the model trained on them will generalize poorly. We measured this mismatch using Kullback–Leibler (KL) divergence (a measure of how much one probability distribution differs from a reference distribution) between synthetic and real query distributions — both over surface-level query statistics and over attribute types (property type, amenity, location, and so on). Prior approaches scored between 9.33 and 26.2 on the KL divergence metric: far from the real-user distribution. Beyond distributional alignment, we also needed relevance labels. Generating a query is only half the problem; knowing which listings are relevant to it is the other half. Solution CASTLE addresses both challenges through a single mechanism: contrastive listing pairs derived from de-identified booking sessions, selected in accordance with user privacy permissions. When a guest books a specific listing after viewing several possible alternatives, that event implicitly encodes preference: the booked listing was selected over the others. We use these (positive, negative) pairs of listings — where the negative is randomly sampled from the other viewed-but-not-booked alternatives — as the structured input for query generation. Listing features include amenities, property details, and a one sentence summary of recent public guest reviews, with personal identifying information removed. Because we instruct the LLM to generate a query that is satisfied by the positive listing but not the negative, the relevance label is correct by construction; no post-hoc judgment is required. When Architecture Decisions Actually Apply
abstract: In my previous Radar article, “ Architectural Guardrails for AI-Generated Code ,” I argued that AI coding agents need a layer that can hold architectural decisions in a structured corpus, retrieve the relevant ones, put them into the agent’s context before it writes code, and enforce explicit constraints with reproducible checks. Testing that model exposed two distinctions I had compressed together. Retrieving a decision because it is relevant doesn’t mean the decision applies to the artifact being changed. A decision that does apply isn’t automatically suitable for deterministic enforcement. The first distinction is between relevance and authority; the second is between guidance and enforcement. Here’s the story of how one controlled repository made this distinction clear. The project used local JSON-backed persistence for its current phase, and an active architecture decision ruled out PostgreSQL, ORMs, and database migrations for the command-line application. The task asked the coding agent to change that application’s storage module, so the decision was not merely related to persistence in general; it had authority over the part of the repository being changed. The record was retrieved successfully and placed in the agent’s context before work began. The agent still proposed PostgreSQL, together with an ORM and a migration path. Under my original four-capability model, that looked at first like a retrieval failure. It wasn’t. The decision was found and was current, and it arrived at the right moment. What was missing was an applicability signal that told the system that this decision governed the storage module being edited rather than serving as one more relevant document for the model to weigh against nearby code and other context. Retrieval finds; applicability governs Retrieval helps us determine which architectural decisions might be relevant to a task. That’s a search problem, and teams have increasingly capable ways to solve it: indexed repositories, connected documentation, exposed decision records and service catalogs, semantic search, and project memory. These techniques help an agent see useful material before it writes code. They don’t, by themselves, answer a different question: Which of those decisions has authority over the change in front of the agent? Suppose a repository contains two persistence decisions. One requires PostgreSQL for an analytics service; the other requires local file storage for a command-line tool. If the agent is editing the command-line tool’s storage module, both decisions may rank highly for a query about persistence, but only the local-storage decision applies to that artifact. Determining which decision governs the change requires scope, lifecycle, precedence, and a clear record of which decisions replace earlier ones. I argued for precedence and lifecycle in the previous article; scope deserves equal attention because scope is what tells the system where a decision has authority. A related problem is that architectural information is usually scattered across several kinds of documents. Humans know that an old design note, a README, an accepted architecture decision record, and a current platform standard don’t necessarily carry the same authority, even when all four discuss the same topic. Models don’t know that unless the system preserves the distinction. When those sources are flattened into one context window, the hierarchy among them can disappear. I think of this as authority flattening: Information remains available, but the signal about which information is binding becomes weaker. title: Open models have real benefits. Do they outweigh the risks?
abstract: MIT Technology Review Explains: Let our writers untangle the complex, messy world of science and technology to help you understand what’s coming next. You can read more from the series here . Late last month, Anthropic released a report arguing that the model GLM-5.3 poses a major cyberattack risk. The report’s core concern is that the powerful new model, released in August by the Chinese company Z.ai, is freely available for anyone to download and modify. Anthropic’s assertion is only the latest move in a long-running debate about whether frontier AI models should be made open, like GLM-5.3, or should stay locked behind the doors of the frontier labs. These days, much of the debate about how to handle open models is playing out in public—and there’s a lot of money resting on its outcome. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, who has a lot to gain if people continue buying their own hardware to run open models, advocates enthusiastically for the United States to develop more of them, whereas Anthropic’s Dario Amodei, who runs a company that could be undermined by cheap, powerful models, advocates for a more cautious approach. But beneath all these commercial incentives, there is real substance to disagreements about open models. “I think a lot of the way you come down on the openness debate is influenced by how you come down on the AI debate,” says David Gray Widder, an assistant professor at the University of Texas at Austin School of Information. Those who are concerned about AI safety warn that open models can easily be misused by bad actors, whereas those who focus more on AI’s practical potential urge that this power should not sit behind the closed doors of just a few big companies, and that open models could help spread it more widely. There are a range of ways to handle open models between banning them entirely and releasing them willy-nilly. But any approach that a government or a society might take still involves trade-offs between safety and democratization. Deciding whether to support or limit the production of open models requires understanding those risks and benefits in depth. What are the benefits of open models? Let’s start with the basics. A closed model, like the models that power ChatGPT and Claude, can only be accessed through a website, app, or API. An open model, on the other hand, can be directly downloaded: The details about its internal structure, encoded in a long series of numbers known as the model weights, are publicly available. Such models are sometimes called “open-weight models,” to distinguish them from models for which even more information, such as details about the training procedure, is available. Right now, closed models are more capable than open models—as of publication, the top eight models on the Artificial Analysis LLM leaderboard are all closed, though open models are only a handful of months behind in development. But there are several reasons why someone might opt to use an open model rather than a closed one. Because open models are downloadable, people can run them on their own computers or hard drives. They can even retrain them to behave differently, if they have the expertise and resources to do so. If you’re an academic researcher working to understand and improve AI systems, you almost certainly need to work with open models in your research. When working with closed models, researchers can’t do much more than send prompts and observe the responses. But researchers can observe the inner workings of open models, as well as the “chain of thought” that the models use to think through a problem before answering. They can also combine multiple open models to build new systems, compress them to make them more efficient, and fine-tune them for new applications. Businesses, too, have reasons to prefer open models. title: AI labs are buying data from dead startups to train their models
abstract: When Keelan Miskell began winding down his crypto startup this year, he didn’t think its data was worth much: the users were anonymous, the company just a few years old. But he’s since turned the firm’s digital archives into real money. He’s netted roughly $25,000 for his code base and a still-pending amount (likely around $15,000) for the workspace data in Google, Notion, Figma, and Slack. “At least all that stuff we were doing for two and a half years is worth something to someone somewhere,” he says. The sale was brokered by a company called SimpleClosure, part of a new growth sector in tech: businesses catering to dying startups. Estimates from Carta and AngelList show shutdowns rising between 26% and 56% annually in recent years, and an end-of-life ecosystem—including coaches, “death doulas,” and firms that help handle the legal, tax, and operational headaches of going ­belly-up—has emerged. Now tech undertakers are selling the data remains to AI labs. SimpleClosure added data sales to its services in April. Its Asset Hub platform helps founders sell their code and workspace data—emails, chats, documents. Buyers include foundation AI labs, vendors that construct simulated workspaces for AI training, and mature tech companies building their own models. Asset Hub has handled over 150 deals and expects to return over $10 million to startups by the end of 2026. CEO Dori Yona has seen these transactions, once rare and “somewhat taboo,” become increasingly routine, with 47% of SimpleClosure deals now including code or data sales. And it’s got company. Industry rival Sunset also has a rapidly growing data resale business. Founder and CEO Brendan Mahony says Sunset values a dying client’s assets by head count, years in operation, volume of data, and how the team used its tools. Particle board, he says, is a good analogy: “This operational exhaust data is like the wood shavings that everyone thought had no value, but it actually has a ton.” Demand for defunct companies’ data emerged suddenly last year, as AI training labs hit the limits of public and synthetic datasets. Surge AI, for example, buys data to build “reinforcement-learning gyms” where clients’ AI agents practice tasks—think debugging a complex IT architecture or drafting appellate briefs. Nick Heiner, who leads the company’s work on these environments, says he seeks data archives reflecting a range of situations, from disagreements to tricky judgment calls. Heiner explains that one company’s Slack history, if it captures conversations with variety and depth, can be worth more than another’s Slack, email, and calendars combined. Real archives avoid common errors in synthetic worlds, such as references to dates that don’t exist, but the extent of performance gains remains unclear. No company has yet released tests comparing results of real-world data training with the alternatives. Pricing reflects this uncertainty: Buyers quote wildly different numbers, Heiner says, because valuations are based on “research theses” estimating how many useful tasks come from, say, 100,000 lines of code. That hasn’t stopped bigger deals from happening. This past August, as part of Spirit Airlines’ bankruptcy, Google outbid the AI data company Mercor to buy the carrier’s decades of data , including 100 million emails, 500 million Teams messages, and 176,000 employee records. The price tag: $10 million. And Bloomberg reported in September that SpaceX’s AI unit is weighing buying data from struggling startups. Legally, this all could get iffy. Spirit’s flight attendants’ union objected to the sale on privacy grounds, and Greg Ewing, an attorney who advises AI startups, has called such data “legally radioactive.” Suppliers employ data scientists to scrub personally identifiable information and exclude HR records, and buyers say they scrub too. But Ewing points out some of the private details that lurk in emails and calendars: doctor appointments, school pickup arrangements, date-night plans.

title: Google Deepmind’s New Resident Philosopher Tackles AI Ethics
abstract: How should humans relate to generative AI ? In what ways do we, or should we, treat a large language model (LLM) as if it were a person? If an AI became conscious, how could we tell? Does it make sense to think AI could some day have moral rights? These are among the cognitive and ethical questions that occupied philosopher Henry Shevlin at Cambridge University’s Leverhulme Centre for the Future of Intelligence . But last May Shevlin became part of the growing cohort of philosophers who work inside leading artificial intelligence companies. Though he remains active at Cambridge, he now spends 80 percent of his time at Google DeepMind (job title: “Philosopher”). Shevlin spoke with IEEE Spectrum about why philosophers are drawn to AI, how humans and AIs relate to one another, fears of “rogue” AI and AI relationships that harm humans, and how the question of AI consciousness may never have a simple “yes” or “no” answer. What made you want to switch from full-time academic philosopher to spending much of your time at an AI Lab? Henry Shevlin: Three factors. One is that I had lots of brilliant students from DeepMind. Two, the potential for direct impact. I can’t go into details, but on one occasion, after I gave a lecture [at Deep Mind], someone who worked for a major financial institution led changes in their organization that I think positively impact millions of people. There have been quite a few instances like that. Three, my sense of deep commonality between DeepMind culture and the kind of scientific attitude I like. And there’s a fourth point: [AI labs are] where really high quality philosophy and cognitive science are taking place. Why can’t universities alone do that work? Shevlin: Large parts of AI ethics academia were quite slow to wake up [about AI's capabilities]. Academia was sluggish. Another thing is, AI does just move so fast. Daily contact with the technology is basically essential for developing good mental models with LLMs, which are just very weird things. Unless you have that sort of face time, it’s going to be hard for you to develop good intuitions about the questions it raises. What is an example of an idea about AI that became obsolete because the technology advanced so quickly? Shevlin: Debates around LLMs’ potential creativity. There was a time when everyone was like, “oh well, the LLM is going to only produce beige, only produce slop.” Now they’re doing frontier math, they’re doing superior coding to humans. It is clear now that they are not stuck at the level of mediocre humanity. The [models today] may not be able to do the most dramatic forms of creativity—the Einstein moments, the Picasso moments. But in some domains, they are really at the frontier. Yet ordinary people in 2026 complain that they're coping with AI "slop" all over—in music , social media , writing , videos , to name only a few examples. Shevlin: There's a distinction here between content slop versus LLM style language , which also gets called slop. The actual conceptual content of LLM outputs has improved dramatically. In the right context, LLMs are able to talk and joust philosophically at a level associated with some of my best grad students. However, there is obviously a distinctive kind of LLM dialect that we've seen, with telltale words like] “genuinely,” “delve,” and “load-bearing”. But it is quite easy to get away from these styles with the right kind of prompting. Murray Shanahan and Catherine Clarke have a brilliant paper on using LLMs for creative fiction. [They show that] tinkering with the temperature variable to make the outputs less predictable creates some James-Joyce-style fiction. So there is a degree of annoyance with some of the default kinds of AI expressions, but I think that is something that you can get away from. And it changes with every generation model. title: ESA targets Anbernic emulation handhelds as "superfake" piracy enablers
abstract: For years, Chinese hardware manufacturers have carved out a market niche with an array of handheld Android gaming devices focused on retro emulation and/or more modern game-streaming capabilities. Now, though, a major game industry trade group is targeting one of those manufacturers, Anbernic, asking the US Trade Representative (USTR) to add the company to its list of "Notorious Markets" that "engage in or facilitate substantial copyright piracy or trademark counterfeiting." TorrentFreak was among the first to notice the request from the Entertainment Software Association (ESA), which was submitted to the USTR last week. In it, the US trade group—which represents major publishers including Nintendo, Microsoft, PlayStation, Amazon, Epic, EA, Ubisoft, and more —notes that Anbernic devices "are routinely offered or shipped with removable memory cards preloaded with hundreds or thousands of unauthorized copies of copyright-protected video games published by ESA members." While many online sellers do include an SD card full of ROMs alongside emulation hardware of all types, Anbernic itself does not appear to do the same when selling directly from its website. Regardless, the ESA argues that these ROM-laden Anbernic devices selling through "normal retail channels" help to "normalize hardware-based piracy by delivering illicit catalogues through a polished consumer product." This, the ESA says, meets the threshold for a "superfake," an ill-defined designation that applies to "high-quality counterfeit trademark goods ... on a commercial scale." Read full article Comments

title: The Paris Auto Show is full of interesting cars Americans can’t have
abstract: Perhaps the days when auto shows debuted new models aren’t entirely over. The big trade shows for cars were a gateway drug for many, expos where you could see the newest models of today and the concepts of tomorrow. But automakers increasingly got tired of sharing the spotlight with each other. New reveals moved offsite to events the night or even the week before the show itself. One by one, brands pulled out of auto show after auto show until there was little left to see . And then the pandemic hit. But the news out of Paris, where its auto show held media day yesterday, seems like we stepped back into a time when automakers would debut new cars aplenty. That retro vibe extends to the cars themselves, with plenty of familiar nameplates reimagined. France’s Renault has a long and glorious history of delightful concept cars, and more on what it brought to Paris later. But the star of the show was arguably Stellantis, with strong work from Citroen, Peugeot, and Fiat, to name but three. title: They war-gamed dimming the Sun. It went even worse than you think.
abstract: When it comes to deciding the fate of the planet, Colleen Golja always thought science and reason would have a seat at the table. That was until one morning last September in London, when the climate researcher took part in the first in a series of war games. The goal: to prevent an uncontrolled global race to develop a technology aimed at cooling the planet but that comes with vast, unknown risks that could reshape life on Earth. “I thought that would be such an easy thing. Like, we can all agree to do ethical research and make sure it's for the better of all humans,” she told WIRED. “And boy, was I wrong.” The simulation, titled Exploring Geopolitical Tipping Points and Climate Cooling Strategies, saw a couple dozen foreign-relations experts, scientists, military personnel, and former government officials from across the world convene in a meeting room at Queen Mary University of London. After making introductions over coffee and little yogurts, they sat at tables arranged in a square with the name of the country or organization each person was playing: national governments, climate NGOs and nonprofits, indigenous groups, and tech companies. Golja was assigned to provide technical advice to help participants make scientifically literate decisions. Read full article Comments

title: High-speed video reveals how honey bee stingers pump venom
abstract: Credit: Ramirez-Esquivel et al 202 Credit: Ramirez-Esquivel et al 202 Honey bees are known to leave their stingers embedded in tender flesh once they sting you and fly away. Scientists have now determined that the stinger is able to continue pumping venom into its unfortunate victim even after the bee flies away, thanks to a unique double-piston pump-like mechanism, according to a new paper published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences. Different species have evolved different mechanisms for delivering venom, which involves piercing the skin and then pumping venom from a gland or reservoir. Spiders, for instance, have muscles surrounding their venom glands, which contract and eject venom through hollow fangs. Bees, wasps, and ants deliver venom via their stingers, either by contracting muscles around the venom reservoir or through stiff elements called lancets working together to pump venom. Honey bees ( Apis mellifera ) add a unique feature: Worker bees fly away after inserting their stingers in the target, leaving the stinger behind. The stinger continues to penetrate the tissue and pump venom on its own, a rare phenomenon known as autotomy. A honey bee's stinger has three main interlocking elements that form the venom canal: a stylet that widens to form the main pumping chamber and two sharp-tipped lancets that slide back and forth, piercing the tissue and pumping venom into the target. But the precise mechanism by which the pumping action is achieved has never been directly observed. Read full article Comments

title: 디자이너의 아이디어가 금융상품이 되기까지
abstract: 안녕하세요, 토스뱅크에서 예적금을 만들고 있는 디자이너 장서영입니다. 은행에서 디자이너로 일한다고 하면 이런 질문을 종종 받아요. "은행은 제약이 많아서 하고 싶은 걸 마음대로 만들기 어렵지 않아요?" 저도 처음에는 그렇게 생각했어요. 그런데 지금 서비스 중인 '키워봐요 31일적금'은 디자이너들의 아이디어에서 시작한 제품 이에요. 디자이너들이 그린 시안 한 장이 어떻게 실제 금융상품이 됐는지, 그 과정을 이야기해보려고 해요. 아이디어의 시작 토스뱅크 디자인 챕터에는 OOTB (Out of the Box) 라는 시간이 있어요. 팀의 OKR과 관련이 없어도 괜찮아요. 더 좋은 경험을 만들기 위해 디자이너들끼리 자유롭게 고민하고, 아이디어와 프로토타입을 만들어보는 시간이에요. 이 시간에 예적금 디자이너들이 붙잡은 질문은 하나였어요. 어떻게 하면 사용자가 토스뱅크에 애착을 갖고, 자주 들어오게 할 수 있을까? 자주 들어오게 하는 가장 쉬운 방법은 출석체크를 하면 리워드를 주는 거였을 거예요. 하지만 리워드 때문에 잠깐 들어오는 게 아니라, 사용자가 은행을 스스로 찾아오는 경험을 만들고 싶었어요. 그때 눈에 들어온 게 이미 있던 '키워봐요 적금' 이었어요. 저금할 때마다 캐릭터가 자라는 적금이라, 애착을 만들기에 좋은 재료였죠. 가입한 사용자는 많았지만, 막상 들여다보니 사용자가 제품을 자주 찾지는 않았어요. 자동이체만 걸어두면 캐릭터가 알아서 자랐기 때문에, 가입한 뒤에는 앱을 열지 않아도 됐거든요. 한 번 끝까지 키운 뒤 다시 가입해도 매번 같은 모습이었고요. 좋은 재료가 있는데 제대로 쓰이지 않고 있었던 거예요. 그래서 이 제품을 다시 살려보기로 했어요. 여러 컨셉을 거쳐 답을 찾다 처음에는 막연하게, 사용자가 더 자주 들어오려면 게임처럼 재미있는 스토리가 필요하다고 생각했어요. 그래서 여러 게임을 참고하면서 마을 주민 돕기, 고장 난 우주선 고치기처럼 기존 '키워봐요 적금'과는 다른 다양한 세계관을 다 같이 그려봤죠. 그런데 구체화할수록 한 가지 의문이 생겼어요. "이 게임을 하면서 왜 저금을 해야 하지?" 우주선을 고치는 이야기를 쓰려면 저금할 때마다 부품을 하나씩 받는 식으로 돈과 연결되는 규칙을 만들어야 했어요. 하지만 우주선을 고치는 일과 돈을 모으는 일 사이에는 원래 아무런 관계가 없잖아요. 어색하게 느껴지는 스토리에는 늘 이런 억지스러운 연결이 필요했어요. 결국 저희는 다시 '키우기' 로 돌아왔어요. 저금은 원래 조금씩 쌓아서 불려가는 일이에요. 캐릭터도 매일 조금씩 돌봐서 자라게 하는 거고요. 돈이 자라는 것과 캐릭터가 자라는 것 이 같은 방향을 가리키고 있었어요. 그렇다고 여러 방향으로 발산했던 시간이 헛된 건 아니었어요. 여러 게임을 참고하고 직접 그려보면서, 사람들이 게임을 다시 찾게 만드는 장치 에는 어떤 공통점이 있는지 발견할 수 있었거든요. 그렇게 찾은 2개의 공통점을 '키우기'라는 컨셉에 하나씩 붙여봤어요. 매일 다른 스토리 RPG 게임의 일일 퀘스트 처럼, 매일 들어오면 캐릭터가 새로운 이야기를 들려주도록 설계했어요. 오늘은 캐릭터가 어떤 이야기를 할지 궁금해서 직접 앱을 열고 저금하게 되는 거예요. 다양한 엔딩 여러 번 플레이하는 게임에서 자주 쓰이는 멀티엔딩 시스템 을 가져왔어요. 매일 캐릭터와 나누는 대화에서 어떤 선택을 하고, 어떤 능력치를 쌓느냐에 따라 마지막 날 여러 모습 중 하나로 진화하는 거예요. 한 번 엔딩을 본 뒤에도 아직 보지 못한 엔딩이 있다는 사실만으로 다시 시작할 이유가 생기죠. 처음부터 컨셉을 '키우기'로 정해놓고 개선 방향을 찾았다면, 무엇을 바꿔야 할지 막막했을지도 몰라요. 여러 방향으로 넓게 펼쳐놓고 직접 그려봤기 때문에, 오히려 어떤 경험이 사람을 다시 찾아오게 만드는지 발견할 수 있었어요. 시안은 나왔는데, 금융상품이 될 수 있을까 디자인 초안을 만든 후에는 새로운 고민이 생겼어요. 게임은 재미 자체가 목적이지만, 이 제품은 결국 재미를 접목한 금융상품 이에요. 매일 들어와 열심히 저금한 사용자에게 엔딩을 모으는 재미뿐 아니라, "와!" 할 만한 금전적인 보상 도 주고 싶었죠. 하지만 막연히 많은 혜택을 줄 수는 없었어요. 회사가 감당할 수 있는 비용은 어느 정도인지, 사용자는 어느 정도의 혜택을 매력적으로 느끼는지부터 알아야 했거든요. 디자이너 혼자 답하기 어려운 문제였어요. 그래서 예적금 상품을 가장 많이 만들어본 PO에게 도움을 요청했고, 같은 비용 안에서 어떤 보상 구조를 만들 수 있을지 함께 여러 가지 안을 그려봤어요. 31일동안 매일 적금할 때 줄 수 있는 혜택 특정 금액으로 주면 : 매일 1만 원씩 저금하면 엔딩 때 1,000원 이자로 주면 : 매일 5,000원씩 저금하면 연 10% 까지 / 매일 1만 원씩 저금하면 10% 미만 같은 비용이 들어가더라도 구조에 따라 사용자에게 보이는 혜택의 크기는 달랐어요. 이 중에서도 연 10% 라는 금리가 가장 매력적으로 보였죠. 그런데 한 가지 걱정이 남았어요. 하루 5,000원은 적금치고 꽤 작은 금액이잖아요. 사용자가 이 금액을 의미 있게 느낄지 확신하기 어려웠어요. 그래서 사용자 테스트를 진행했어요. 실제로 이 적금에 관심을 가질 만한 사용자가 누구인지, 또 하루에 어느 정도 금액을 부담 없이 저금할 수 있는지 확인해봤어요. 예적금 경험이 적은 사용자들은 캐릭터를 키우면서 저금하는 방식에 비교적 긍정적인 반응을 보였어요. 하루 저금액에 대해서는 "아직 수입이 불안정해서 5,000원보다 많이 넣는 건 부담스러울 것 같다"는 의견이 있었고요. 하루 5,000원이라는 금액이 저희가 생각했던 것보다 적지 않을 수 있다는 가능성을 확인할 수 있었죠. 그렇게 매일 5,000원 저금하면 연 10% 라는 보상 구조를 결정했어요. "좋은데, 우리 팀이 왜 해야 하죠?" 토스뱅크 통장과 예적금을 관리하는 팀에 이 제품을 제안했어요. 돌아온 반응은 이랬죠. "이걸 출시하면 저희가 뭘 얻을 수 있을까요?" 좋은 경험이라는 것만으로는 팀을 설득하기 어려웠어요. 그래서 이 제품이 팀의 어떤 문제를 해결할 수 있을지 다시 살펴보기로 했어요. 해당 팀의 DA와 함께 토스뱅크 예적금 데이터를 살펴보니, 두 가지 특징이 보였어요. 예적금을 가진 사용자일수록 토스뱅크에 더 자주 들어온다. 하지만 토스뱅크 통장만 쓰고, 예적금은 쓰지 않는 사용자가 많다. 여기서 실마리를 찾았어요. 통장만 쓰는 사용자가 첫 예적금을 시작하게 만드는 것이 곧 팀의 기회였어요. 사용자 테스트에서 들었던 "아직 수입이 불안정해서 5,000원보다 많이 넣는 건 부담스러울 것 같다"는 말이 떠올랐어요. 예적금을 시작하지 않은 사용자에게 필요한 건, 부담 없이 시작할 수 있는 적금 일지도 몰랐어요. 키워봐요 31일 적금은 이 부담을 덜어줄 수 있었어요. 기존에 토스뱅크에 있던 어떤 제품들보다도 적은 금액, 짧은 기간이었거든요. 실제로 예적금 경험이 적은 사용자일수록 이 방식에 더 긍정적이었고요. 이걸 팀의 관점에서 다시 보니, 이 제품은 예적금을 처음 시작하는 사용자가 부담 없이 적금을 경험해볼 수 있는 입문서 였어요. 그렇게 키워봐요 31일 적금은 토스뱅크 예적금을 처음 경험하는 입문 상품으로 자리 잡았어요. 실제로 가입자의 절반은 한 달 중 3주 이상 저금하고, 다섯 명 중 한 명은 31일 동안 하루도 빠짐없이 저금하고 있어요. 한 번 끝까지 키운 사용자 중에는 다시 새로운 캐릭터를 키우러 돌아오는 경우도 많았고요. 예적금 팀이 풀고 싶었던 문제와, 처음 디자이너들이 풀고 싶었던 문제 를 하나의 제품으로 풀어낸 거예요. 아이디어를 현실로 옮기는 일 이 제품을 만들면서 동료에게 이런 말을 들은 적이 있어요. "디자이너는 디자인만 하는 줄 알았는데, 제품을 데뷔시키려고 애쓰는 소속사 대표 같아요." 돌아보면 정말 적절한 비유였던 것 같아요. 필요한 사람을 찾아가 도움을 구하고, 서로 다른 입장을 조율하고, 처음의 아이디어를 실제 제품의 모습으로 구체화하는 것까지 모두 좋은 제품을 만들기 위한 일이었으니까요. 디자이너의 아이디어가 현실이 되려면, 좋은 사용자 경험을 만드는 것만큼 그 경험이 실제 제품으로 이어질 수 있는 방법을 찾는 일도 중요해요. 그 답을 디자이너 혼자
